Random numbers

Source: vignettes/random.Rmd
random.Rmd
library(jaxR)

jaxR ports jax.random. It does not use R’s global random number stream (set.seed() has no effect on it). Random functions are pure: each one takes a key, and the same key always gives the same numbers. This is what makes random code safe under jit, vmap and grad. The generator is the counter based Threefry 2x32 hash, and its bits agree with JAX exactly: a key built from seed 0 gives the random bits and integers that jax.random gives in Python. Float samples are computed from those bits, so they agree to the rounding of the floating point functions involved (a few units in the last place).

Keys

random_key() builds a key from an integer seed.

key <- random_key(0L)
key
#> Array((), dtype=key<fry>) overlaying:
#> Array u32[2]
#> [1] 0 0
random_normal(key, 3L)
#> Array f32[3]
#> [1]  1.6226422  2.0252647 -0.4335944
random_normal(key, 3L)      # same key, same numbers
#> Array f32[3]
#> [1]  1.6226422  2.0252647 -0.4335944

Never use a key twice for values that must be independent. Derive new keys with random_split(); it returns an array of keys that you index like any other array.

keys <- random_split(key, 3L)
dim(keys)
#> [1] 3
random_normal(keys[0], 2L)
#> Array f32[2]
#> [1]  1.0040143 -0.9063372
random_normal(keys[1], 2L)
#> Array f32[2]
#> [1] -2.442456 -2.035681

The usual pattern in a loop is to split the carried key at each step:

key <- random_key(42L)
draws <- numeric(3)
for (i in 1:3) {
  ks <- random_split(key)
  key <- ks[0]
  draws[i] <- as.numeric(random_uniform(ks[1]))
}
draws
#> [1] 0.7276642 0.4164864 0.3464590

random_fold_in(key, data) derives a key from a key and an integer, which is convenient when a natural index exists (an iteration number, a layer number):

random_normal(random_fold_in(key, 7L), 2L)
#> Array f32[2]
#> [1] 0.2440771759 0.0004393304

Typed keys and raw keys

random_key() returns a typed key array (dtype key<fry>). random_PRNGKey() returns the legacy representation, a uint32 array of shape 2. Both work with every sampler. random_key_data() and random_wrap_key_data() convert between the two, and random_key_impl() names the generator.

random_key_data(random_key(1L))
#> Array u32[2]
#> [1] 0 1
random_PRNGKey(1L)
#> Array u32[2]
#> [1] 0 1
random_key_impl(random_key(1L))
#> [1] "threefry2x32"
k <- random_wrap_key_data(as_jax(c(0L, 1L), "uint32"))
dtype(k)
#> [1] "key<fry>"

Other generators are available through impl: "threefry2x32" (the default), "rbg" and "unsafe_rbg". The default can be changed with jax_config_update("jax_default_prng_impl", "rbg").

random_normal(random_key(0L, impl = "rbg"), 2L)
#> Array f32[2]
#> [1] -0.255816  1.177591

Samplers

Every sampler takes the key first, then distribution parameters where they exist, then the output shape and dtype.

key <- random_key(2026L)
k <- random_split(key, 12L)

random_uniform(k[0], c(2L, 3L), minval = -1, maxval = 1)
#> Array f32[2,3]
#>            [,1]        [,2]          [,3]
#> [1,]  0.2841105 -0.94586730 -0.4288947582
#> [2,] -0.8597288 -0.04625559  0.0005886555
random_normal(k[1], 4L, dtype = "float32")
#> Array f32[4]
#> [1] -1.2562261 -0.7791061  1.2774522  2.1839666
random_randint(k[2], 5L, minval = 0L, maxval = 10L)
#> Array i32[5]
#> [1] 9 4 9 7 1
random_bernoulli(k[3], p = 0.3, shape = 6L)
#> Array bool[6]
#> [1] FALSE FALSE FALSE  TRUE FALSE FALSE
random_exponential(k[4], 3L)
#> Array f32[3]
#> [1] 0.5577374 0.1386228 0.5270879
random_gamma(k[5], a = 2, shape = 3L)
#> Array f32[3]
#> [1] 1.0319114 0.5817389 1.0481006
random_beta(k[6], a = 2, b = 5, shape = 3L)
#> Array f32[3]
#> [1] 0.2961964 0.2967143 0.4720042
random_poisson(k[7], lam = 4, shape = 5L)
#> Array i32[5]
#> [1] 1 3 3 6 3
random_categorical(k[8], logits = jnp_log(c(0.1, 0.6, 0.3)), shape = 8L)
#> Array i32[8]
#> [1] 1 2 1 1 1 2 2 2
random_truncated_normal(k[9], lower = -1, upper = 1, shape = 4L)
#> Array f32[4]
#> [1]  0.95993203 -0.69172060 -0.07682008  0.29111522

Distribution parameters broadcast against each other and against shape:

random_gamma(k[10], a = c(0.5, 5, 50))
#> Array f32[3]
#> [1]  0.04255044  7.95875216 61.38506317

The full list of samplers:

Family Functions
Uniform and integer random_uniform, random_randint, random_bits
Gaussian family random_normal, random_truncated_normal, random_multivariate_normal, random_lognormal, random_generalized_normal
Discrete random_bernoulli, random_binomial, random_categorical, random_geometric, random_multinomial, random_poisson, random_rademacher
Gamma family random_gamma, random_loggamma, random_beta, random_chisquare, random_dirichlet, random_f, random_t
Heavy tails and extremes random_cauchy, random_pareto, random_gumbel, random_laplace, random_logistic, random_weibull_min, random_wald
Physics random_maxwell, random_double_sided_maxwell, random_rayleigh, random_triangular
Geometry random_ball, random_orthogonal
Combinatorial random_choice, random_permutation

Multivariate draws 

mu <- c(0, 1)
Sigma <- matrix(c(1, 0.8, 0.8, 1), 2)
x <- random_multivariate_normal(k[11], mu, Sigma, shape = 2000L)
dim(x)
#> [1] 2000    2
jnp_cov(x, rowvar = FALSE)
#> Array f32[2,2]
#>           [,1]      [,2]
#> [1,] 1.0039188 0.8184109
#> [2,] 0.8184109 1.0373667

random_dirichlet(key, alpha = c(1, 2, 3), shape = 2L)
#> Array f32[2,3]
#>            [,1]      [,2]      [,3]
#> [1,] 0.03309954 0.6385041 0.3283964
#> [2,] 0.18649434 0.1698514 0.6436542
Q <- random_orthogonal(key, 3L)
jnp_round(Q %*% jnp_transpose(Q), 4L)
#> Array f32[3,3]
#>      [,1] [,2] [,3]
#> [1,]    1    0    0
#> [2,]    0    1    0
#> [3,]    0    0    1

Permutations and choices 

random_permutation(key, 6L)
#> Array i32[6]
#> [1] 0 1 4 5 2 3
random_permutation(key, as_jax(c(10, 20, 30, 40)))
#> Array f32[4]
#> [1] 10 20 30 40
random_choice(key, as_jax(c(10, 20, 30, 40)), shape = 3L, replace = FALSE)
#> Array f32[3]
#> [1] 10 20 30
random_choice(key, 4L, shape = 6L, p = c(0.7, 0.1, 0.1, 0.1))
#> Array i32[6]
#> [1] 0 0 0 0 1 0

Random numbers and transformations

Samplers are ordinary jaxR functions, so they compile, vectorize and differentiate.

# jit: the key is an argument, so one compiled function serves every key
sample_mean <- jit(function(key) jnp_mean(random_normal(key, 1000L)))
sample_mean(random_key(1L))
#> Array f32[]
#> [1] -0.02815822
sample_mean(random_key(2L))
#> Array f32[]
#> [1] 0.02009065

# vmap over a batch of keys: independent streams, one compiled kernel
keys <- random_split(random_key(0L), 4L)
vmap(function(k) random_normal(k, 3L))(keys)
#> Array f32[4,3]
#>            [,1]       [,2]       [,3]
#> [1,]  1.0040143 -0.9063372 -0.7481722
#> [2,] -2.4424558 -2.0356805  0.2055442
#> [3,]  1.2956359  1.3550105 -0.4096056
#> [4,] -0.6219436  0.6248041  1.6820775

Samplers that have a differentiable reparameterization propagate gradients with respect to their parameters. The gradient of a gamma draw with respect to its shape parameter is computed by implicit differentiation, as in JAX:

grad(function(a) random_gamma(random_key(0L), a))(2.5)
#> Array f32[] weak_type
#> [1] 0.9727995
grad(function(s) jnp_mean(s * random_normal(random_key(0L), 100L)^2))(1.5)
#> Array f32[] weak_type
#> [1] 0.8983123

Checking key reuse

Drawing twice from one key gives the same numbers, which is rarely intended. With the option jax_debug_key_reuse (port of jax.experimental.key_reuse), a key that a random function used is consumed, and passing a consumed key again is an error of class jax_key_reuse_error. random_split() consumes its key and returns new ones; random_fold_in() and random_key_data() do not consume; random_clone() returns an unconsumed copy. Indexing a key array consumes the keys it selects.

debug_key_reuse(TRUE, {
  key <- random_key(0)
  x <- random_normal(key)
  tryCatch(random_normal(key), jax_key_reuse_error = function(e) conditionMessage(e))
})
#> [1] "Previously-consumed key passed to random_bits at index 0"

The check follows keys through jit() (a function that consumes an argument or a key it closes over consumes it at every call), lax_cond(), vmap() and the loops: a lax_scan() or lax_while_loop() body must make a new key for its carry instead of consuming the carried one every iteration.

debug_key_reuse(TRUE, {
  body <- function(key, x) {
    ks <- as.list(random_split(key))
    list(ks[[1]], random_uniform(ks[[2]]))
  }
  ok <- lax_scan(body, random_key(1), NULL, length = 3L)[[2]]
  bad <- tryCatch(lax_scan(function(k, x) list(k, random_uniform(k)), random_key(1), NULL,
                           length = 3L),
                  jax_key_reuse_error = function(e) conditionMessage(e))
  list(ok = ok, bad = bad)
})
#> $ok
#> Array f32[3]
#> [1] 0.4036463 0.8283720 0.5436133
#> 
#> $bad
#> [1] "scan body function leads to key reuse when repeatedly executed, because consumed inputs don't match sourced outputs"

A stateful generator

Explicit keys are the recommended way to draw random numbers, because the state is visible. For code translated from NumPy there is also a generator whose state updates implicitly: experimental_random_stateful_rng() (the port of jax.experimental.random.stateful_rng), in the style of numpy.random.default_rng. It holds a key and a counter in a mutable reference; each draw folds the counter into the key and adds one to the counter.

rng <- experimental_random_stateful_rng(42)
rng$uniform()
#> Array f32[]
#> [1] 0.5302608
rng$uniform()
#> Array f32[]
#> [1] 0.7276642
rng$normal(loc = 10, scale = 2, size = 3L)
#> Array f32[3]
#> [1] 10.864613 11.174528  7.716651
rng$integers(0L, 10L, size = 5L)
#> Array i32[5]
#> [1] 6 4 5 6 5
rng$random(c(2L, 2L))
#> Array f32[2,2]
#>           [,1]      [,2]
#> [1,] 0.7437396 0.5688519
#> [2,] 0.9454045 0.7802591

size is an integer, an integer vector, or NULL for the broadcast shape of the parameters. rng$key() hands out a fresh explicit key (rng$key(4L) an array of keys), for functions that want one:

random_gamma(rng$key(), 2.5, 3L)
#> Array f32[3]
#> [1] 1.0163749 0.6584333 2.8018618
rng$counter[]
#> Array i32[]
#> [1] 6

The generator works inside transformations. jit threads the counter through the compiled function, so repeated calls give new draws:

noisy <- jit(function(x) x + rng$normal(size = 2L))
noisy(jnp_zeros(2L))
#> Array f32[2]
#> [1] -0.2544037 -0.6385937
noisy(jnp_zeros(2L))
#> Array f32[2]
#> [1]  0.288639694 -0.009632921

For vmap, split the generator: rng$split(n) is one generator holding n independent children, and each mapped call advances its own child. rng$spawn(n) returns the children as a list of separate generators instead.

children <- rng$split(3L)
vmap(function(r, x) x + r$uniform())(children, jnp_zeros(3L))
#> Array f32[3]
#> [1] 0.7198955 0.5716037 0.5674410
children$counter[]
#> Array i32[3]
#> [1] 1 1 1
kids <- rng$spawn(2L)
kids[[1L]]$integers(10L, size = 2L)
#> Array i32[2]
#> [1] 9 7

Without a seed the generator is seeded from R’s random number generator, so set.seed() makes it reproducible; inside a transformed function a seed is required. Because the counter is a reference, a generator cannot be returned from a function compiled with jit, and so it cannot be a carry of lax_scan or lax_while_loop; a generator that the body closes over works.

A worked example: Monte Carlo integration

The estimate of π\pi from points in the unit square, vectorized over independent replications:

estimate_pi <- jit(function(key) {
  u <- random_uniform(key, c(20000L, 2L))
  4 * jnp_mean(jnp_sum(u^2, axis = 1L) < 1)
})
reps <- vmap(estimate_pi)(random_split(random_key(123L), 8L))
reps
#> Array f32[8]
#> [1] 3.1256 3.1390 3.1396 3.1456 3.1364 3.1426 3.1474 3.1198
jnp_mean(reps)
#> Array f32[]
#> [1] 3.137

Agreement with JAX

Because the generator and every sampling algorithm are ported exactly, a jaxR program and its JAX counterpart produce the same draws from the same seed. In Python, jax.random.normal(jax.random.key(0), (3,)) gives the values printed by the first chunk of this vignette. The test suite checks this for every sampler against values produced by JAX.
